title: Catt Spiral Revival: Wafer-Scale Memory From Rejected DRAM Wafers
idea: Revive Ivor Catt's 1989 Anamartic self-organizing spiral wafer: instead of dicing rejected or partial-yield DRAM wafers, probe-map every die, bond a small harvest-controller chiplet per reticle field, and let a boot-time 'spiral' protocol chain only the good dies into a serial-linked string that a host sees as one wafer-scale CXL memory slab of 100-300 GB.
why: Scarce-resource and cost per bit: salvages wafers and dies now scrapped or down-binned for a few defects (plus HBM-stack yield losses of 20-30%); claimed +5-10% effective bit supply at near-zero capex.

title: Sinclair Half-Good Chips: Sell Partial-Capacity DRAM Die With Fuse Maps
idea: Revive the 1982 ZX Spectrum trick of shipping TI 4532 'half-good' 64K chips: dies that exhaust their repair fuses in one bank-half are fused to a clean half-capacity address map and sold as standard 12/24 Gb SKUs for edge, IoT, consoles and appliances, with a JEDEC 'partial-good' mode register so controllers need no special handling.
why: Cost per bit and supply: recovers dies currently scrapped after redundancy exhaustion (several % of gross dies, more during early node ramps), ~3-8% more sellable bits per wafer and full dies freed for servers.

title: ARAM Revival: Retention-Weak DRAM Grade for Error-Tolerant AI Tensors
idea: Revive 1980s 'audio RAM' (known-defective DRAM sold cheaply for answering machines) as a T-grade tier: dies that fail 64 ms retention but pass at 8-16 ms, or have clustered stuck bits, ship with a defect bitmap in SPD; the memory controller refreshes them faster and the scheduler places only error-tolerant data (activations, KV caches, gradient buffers) there while masking mapped bits.
why: Supply: the retention tail is a major test-reject category; converting it into usable capacity adds ~2-5% bits and a ~50%-price tier without new wafers.

title: IBM MXT Revival: Hardware Memory Compression Inside CXL Expanders
idea: Revive IBM's 2000 Memory eXpansion Technology (the Pinnacle controller: parallel LZ compression of 1 KB blocks into sectored storage with a decompressed-line cache) inside CXL Type-3 expander controllers, with a per-page translation table and an on-controller SRAM line cache so the OS simply sees about twice the capacity.
why: Usable supply: MXT measured ~2x on real server data; a 1.8-2.5x effective capacity on the pooled tier is equivalent to doubling DRAM output for that tier with zero new fab capacity.

title: Staktek-Style Package Stacking to Bypass the TSV Bottleneck
idea: Revive the 1990s Staktek/Dense-Pac technique of stacking finished, fully tested packages with flex-frame rails: towers of 4-8 conventional wire-bonded DDR5 packages per site build 256-512 GB capacity RDIMMs on ordinary OSAT lines instead of TSV lines.
why: HBM TSV tax: TSV stacks use ~3x the wafer area per bit and lose 20-30% yield; package stacking uses standard dies, known-good packages and idle OSAT capacity for the capacity tier, freeing TSV capacity for HBM.

title: Irvine Sensors Edge-Cube: Side-Metallized Die Stacks Instead of TSVs
idea: Revive Irvine Sensors' 1990s 'memory cube': thin 16-32 known-good DRAM dies, glue them into a block, lap one face to expose pads rerouted to the die edge, and pattern the interconnect directly on that side face with laser direct-write metallization, giving a high-capacity stack with no through-silicon vias at all.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield: no TSV keep-out area or TSV process (recovering much of the ~3x area-per-bit penalty), KGD tested before stacking; lets U.S. defense and OSAT packagers make capacity stacks.

title: FB-DIMM AMB Reborn: Adapter Lets Reclaimed DDR3/DDR4 Join Modern Servers
idea: Revive the abandoned 2007 Fully-Buffered DIMM Advanced Memory Buffer as a cheap serial/CXL buffer chip on refurbished boards that host reclaimed DDR3/DDR4 chips, translating timing, voltage and protocol so decommissioned memory becomes a second-life capacity tier in new servers.
why: Supply and scarce resources: hundreds of millions of GB sit in retired servers; reuse at ~10-20% of new-bit cost can cover 10%+ of cold-data demand.

title: Rajchman Apertured Ferrite Plates Printed on MLCC Production Lines
idea: Revive Jan Rajchman's 1950s RCA batch-fabricated apertured ferrite plate memory by screen-printing and co-firing nano-ferrite layers with embedded silver drive and sense windings on multilayer-ceramic-capacitor lines (which already print trillions of layered parts a year), giving non-volatile, refresh-free, byte-addressable blocks with ~100-300 ns access.
why: Capital and scarce resources: zero EUV, iron-oxide and silver chemistry, existing MLCC tool base (including U.S. plants); low density but near-zero capex for refresh-free industrial and edge memory that frees DRAM.

title: Twistor Revival on Magnetic-Tape Coating Lines
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1957 twistor (magnetic tape wrapped helically on a sense wire) as laminated sheets: surviving data-tape coating lines deposit high-coercivity barium-ferrite stripes on PET film over printed copper sense lines, then laminate crossed drive-line films roll-to-roll at km per hour.
why: Capital intensity: a roll-to-roll web line costs ~$50M versus a $15B fab and reuses the LTO tape industry; yields a non-volatile slow working-memory tier to absorb cold DRAM pages.

title: Williams Tube 2.0: Field-Emitter Arrays From Abandoned FED Display Lines
idea: Revive the 1947 Williams tube (bits as charge spots on a dielectric written and read by an electron beam) using the field-emission-display tooling Candescent and Sony abandoned: each microtip emitter addresses a 1-4 um patch of unpatterned charge-storage film, read back by secondary-emission sensing, so cell density is set by beam focus rather than lithography.
why: Litho-bound scaling and capital: the storage film needs no patterning or EUV, and mothballed display vacuum lines supply the emitter arrays.

title: Bubble-Memory One-Mask Recipe Revived With Skyrmion Multilayers in Micro-Fabs
idea: Revive Intel Magnetics' 1980s bubble-memory recipe, a magnetic film plus a single permalloy overlay mask, but replace bubbles with room-temperature skyrmions in sputtered Pt/Co/Ir multilayer tracks moved by current pulses, so a chip needs one nanoimprint layer plus readout tunnel junctions and can be made in ~$100M micro-fabs.
why: Capital intensity: 1-2 patterning layers versus ~70 DRAM masks including 5-7 EUV; enables distributed U.S. micro-fabs for a serial-access capacity tier.

title: Intel 1103 Strategy: 3T Gain-Cell DRAM on Idle Mature Logic Fabs
idea: Revive the capacitor-free three-transistor cell of Intel's 1970 1103 on idle 28-65 nm 300 mm logic lines, using a standard logic flow plus a raised-Vt write device, and sell it as 'commodity-lite' DRAM chiplets for capacity tiers, letting a startup ramp the way Intel did with the 1103.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: no capacitor module or EUV, uses depreciated fabs (depreciation is ~55% of DRAM wafer cost); cost per bit ~2-3x higher than 1a DRAM but available now from existing U.S. capacity.

title: VLSI Research Association Redux: U.S. Cooperative for EUV-Free DRAM
idea: Revive Japan's 1976-80 VLSI Technology Research Association, where five rivals shared one joint lab and built the steppers and e-beam tools that won DRAM: a time-boxed U.S. cooperative of a memory maker, tool vendors, hyperscalers and national labs co-develops patent-pooled DUV/nanoimprint DRAM process modules, then disbands so members compete on products.
why: Capital and litho: shares the ~$5B R&D for a non-EUV DRAM flow; Japan's version helped move its DRAM share to a majority within a decade.

title: Fair-Market-Value Floor Revived: Offtake Price Corridor for New DRAM Fabs
idea: Revive the 1986 U.S.-Japan Semiconductor Agreement's fair-market-value price floors as a 10-year price corridor: hyperscalers and the government sign take-or-pay contracts with new-entrant fabs at a floor and a cap per Gb, and a stabilization fund pays the difference during gluts and is refilled during spikes.
why: Capital intensity: the bust half of the cycle is what kills new fabs; a floor cuts the cost of capital by several points and makes a $15B fab bankable.

title: Federal Helium Reserve Reborn, With Fab Priority and Recapture Mandates
idea: Re-create the Bush Dome Federal Helium Reserve sold off in 2024 as a strategic semiconductor helium bank: buy North American helium in normal years, re-inject it at Cliffside, release it to fabs under priority rules in shocks, and pair it with grants for closed-loop helium recapture on litho, wafer-cooling and leak-check tools.
why: Scarce resources: Qatar (~30% of supply) offline since March 2026; recapture cuts fab helium use 50-90% and the reserve buffers multi-year disruptions.

title: Skull-Melting Silicon: Cold-Crucible Czochralski Without Spruce Pine Quartz
idea: Revive the Lebedev Institute's 1970s skull-melting technique (cold-crucible induction melting, used to make cubic zirconia) for silicon crystal growth: a water-cooled segmented copper crucible inductively melts silicon that freezes into its own thin solid-silicon skull, so no high-purity quartz crucible ever touches the melt.
why: Scarce resource: removes the Spruce Pine >80% high-purity-quartz crucible chokepoint, lowers oxygen contamination, and turns the crucible into reusable copper.

title: IBM 650 SOAP Revival: Time-Placing Tensors so Flash Replaces DRAM
idea: Revive the 1955 Symbolic Optimal Assembly Program, which placed each instruction on the drum so it arrived under the read head just when needed: a compiler for static AI graphs lays out every weight and KV block across NAND/SSD stripes so it streams in just in time through a small DRAM staging ring.
why: Usable supply: replaces most resident-weight DRAM with flash at ~10-20x lower cost per bit; DRAM per served model can drop 5-10x.

title: Intel-AMD 1982 Second-Source Rule Applied to DRAM Designs
idea: Revive the IBM and DoD rule of the 1970s-80s that every critical chip have a licensed second source: federal buyers and a hyperscaler purchasing consortium qualify a DRAM product only if it is licensed, with design-kit and process escrow, to a second, geographically separate fab.
why: Supply resilience and U.S. manufacturability: creates guaranteed demand for a second U.S. fab and spreads know-how; the x86 second-source deal is what created AMD's fab business.

title: Liberty Fab: One Frozen DRAM Fab Design Copied by Many Builders
idea: Revive WWII Liberty-ship production (one frozen design built by 18 yards, cutting build time from ~230 to ~40 days) for memory: a frozen, open DRAM fab blueprint (building, tool set, DUV-only mature 1y-class recipe) is replicated modularly by several contractors and operators who share learning-curve data.
why: Capital and time: design reuse and cross-copy learning cut fab build time from 3-5 years toward ~18 months and capex by ~30%.

title: Arsenal Conversion: Idle Gen-8 LCD Lines Make Oxide Memory Panels
idea: Revive the WWII conversion of car plants into bomber plants: buy shuttered Gen-8.5 LCD TFT fabs and convert their IGZO backplane process to build 2T0C oxide gain-cell memory arrays on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass panels, diced into low-cost capacity chiplets.
why: Capital: one glass panel has ~70x the area of a 300 mm wafer at a fraction of the cost per area; repurposes stranded display capex instead of building fabs.

title: IBM Lease-and-Reclaim: DRAM-as-a-Service With Guaranteed Return
idea: Revive IBM's mainframe-era model in which IBM owned and recovered every core-memory box: memory makers lease modules to data centers with mandatory return at end of term, then retest, rebin and re-lease them into lower tiers (inference, CXL cold pools, edge).
why: Supply: extends each bit's productive life from ~5 to 10+ years, cutting new-bit demand, while makers capture the refurbishment margin.

title: Ever-Normal Granary for Bits: Strategic DRAM Wafer Buffer Stock
idea: Revive the 1930s ever-normal granary and the Cold War National Defense Stockpile for memory: a government corporation buys finished, tested DRAM wafers in die-bank form (stored under dry nitrogen) during gluts at floor prices and sells them into shortages, holding about three months of national demand.
why: Supply volatility: shaves 4x price spikes and keeps fabs at full utilization in busts, lowering cost per bit ~10-15% over the cycle.

title: NEC 4-Level DRAM Revival With Setun Balanced-Ternary Storage
idea: Revive NEC's 1997 four-level 4 Gb DRAM and the Soviet Setun's balanced-ternary memory: store three levels (-, 0, +) around the VDD/2 bitline precharge so the 0 state needs no charge, sensed by a two-step sense amplifier with a reference half-cell, giving 1.58 bits per cell on an unchanged capacitor.
why: Density and cost per bit: ~58% more bits per wafer on existing fabs without new litho; only two thresholds are sensed, easing the 5 fF charge wall versus 4-level designs.

title: Goto's Parametron Revived as Resonant Charge-Recovery DRAM Wordline Drivers
idea: Revive Eiichi Goto's 1954 parametron (resonant LC circuits that ran Japan's PC-1 computer) as on-package inductor tanks that swing DRAM wordlines and bitline groups sinusoidally over a ~10 ns window and return their charge to the tank instead of dumping it to ground, recovering 80-90% of CV2.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): CV2 on ~3 V wordlines and ~1 V bitlines dominates array energy; adiabatic recovery gives ~5-10x lower array energy per access; a periphery-only change licensable to every existing DRAM fab.

title: Crowe Cell Revival on SkyWater's U.S. Superconducting Process
idea: Revive J.W. Crowe's 1957 persistent-current cell, a bit stored as a circulating supercurrent in a niobium loop, on the 200 mm niobium superconducting processes already run in U.S. foundries, read by SQUIDs, to build attojoule-access memory banks for cryogenic AI and quantum data centers.
why: Energy per access ~1000x lower at chip level (aJ-fJ), still ~10x lower after cryocooler overhead; made in U.S. fabs with 250 nm-class litho and no EUV.

title: ETA-10 Revival: Liquid-Nitrogen Pods for Commodity DRAM at 77 K
idea: Revive ETA Systems' 1987 liquid-nitrogen-immersed CMOS supercomputer: immerse standard DRAM in LN2 pods (nitrogen is abundant, unlike helium), where leakage collapses so retention reaches minutes and refresh is switched off, the steeper subthreshold slope lets VARY and wordline drop to ~0.4/1.2 V, and copper resistance falls ~7x.
why: Energy per access: V2 cut ~6-8x, wire RC ~7x lower, refresh gone, net ~10x lower energy per access; also returns the 10-20% of bandwidth lost to refresh, using existing chips and a new packaging business.

title: Dual-Port VRAM Revival: Serial Access Port Streams Entire DRAM Rows
idea: Revive the 1980s video RAM serial access memory (SAM) port: each bank gets a row-wide shift register that captures a full 8 KB row in one activation and streams it out through a narrow low-swing port, so weight and KV streams use 100% of each opened row instead of one 64 B burst.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): a random read costs ~5.9 pJ per useful bit because of 128x overfetch; consuming whole rows cuts activation energy per useful bit 50-100x and total access energy ~10x; buildable on existing DDR4/DDR5 lines with periphery changes only.

title: CCD Memory Revival in Retiring Image-Sensor Foundries
idea: Revive Fairchild and Intel's 1970s CCD serial memory: charge packets clocked through buried-channel shift registers at low swing in loop-organized blocks with regeneration each lap, built on the CCD image-sensor lines now being retired, to serve sequential weight and KV-cache streams.
why: Energy per access: moving a 10k-electron packet costs aJ-fJ per stage versus pJ for bitline swing and sensing, ~10-30x lower per streamed bit; reuses depreciated fabs with no capacitor module.

title: Bucket-Brigade Analog Storage: 6-Bit Charge Packets Per Cell
idea: Revive the 1969 Philips bucket-brigade device (the analog delay chip in guitar pedals) as multi-level analog charge storage for low-precision AI activations: each capacitor holds one of 64 charge levels, read by a shared successive-approximation ADC per column, built on mature 180-65 nm analog/mixed-signal fabs.
why: Energy and density per useful bit: one charge transfer carries 6 bits (6x fewer cell operations) at small swing (2-3x less than full restore), about 10x lower energy per bit; adds analog-fab capacity to memory supply.

title: Mercury Delay Line Reborn as a Fiber Loop Broadcasting Weights
idea: Revive EDSAC's 1949 mercury delay line as a recirculating optical-fiber loop: a model's weights circulate as WDM pulses in a ~100 km fiber spool (100 wavelengths at 400 Gb/s hold ~2.5 GB, one lap every 0.5 ms) with an amplifier-regenerator, and dozens of accelerators tap the loop through passive splitters, each reading every weight once per lap, matching per-token decode cadence.
why: Replaces N per-accelerator DRAM weight copies with one in-flight copy and amortizes each weight access over N readers: ~10-50x lower energy per access at N>=32; built from telecom optics supply chains, not DRAM fabs.

title: Core-Rope ROM for Frozen Model Weights in Mature Fabs
idea: Revive Apollo's core rope memory, where the program was woven into the hardware: frozen foundation-model weights are written into via-programmed multi-level ROM chiplets (one custom via mask per model on a 28-40 nm mature line), read with small-swing sensing and no refresh or row restore, stacked beside the accelerator.
why: Energy per access ~10x lower than DRAM (~0.3 pJ/bit, no activation, restore or refresh); frees the large share of inference DRAM that only holds static weights, using mature-fab capacity.

title: Zuse's Relay Memory as Nano-Relays on TI's DLP MEMS Lines
idea: Revive the electromechanical relay memory of Zuse's Z3 as bistable nanoelectromechanical contact relays (latched by a hold electrode) built on mature MEMS-mirror lines such as TI's DLP fab in Dallas: zero off-state leakage and abrupt switching at ~0.2 V, so cells need no refresh and bitlines swing tiny voltages.
why: Energy per access: CV2 at 0.2 V versus 1-3 V is 25-200x lower and zero leakage removes refresh (fact 3); claimed >=10x lower energy per access from existing U.S. MEMS capacity.

title: Esaki Diode Revival: Goto-Pair RTD Memory on Phone RF GaAs Fabs
idea: Revive the 1958 Esaki tunnel diode and Goto's tunnel-diode-pair memory as resonant-tunneling-diode bistable cells (two series RTDs plus one HEMT access device) running at 0.3 V, made on the GaAs/InP lines that build smartphone RF front ends in North Carolina, Massachusetts and Oregon.
why: Energy per access ~10x lower via 0.3 V swing and static, refresh-free storage with nW standby; adds memory supply from underused III-V RF fab capacity.

title: Magnetostrictive Delay Line Reborn as YIG Magnon Loops on Bubble-Memory Lines
idea: Revive the nickel-wire magnetostrictive delay lines of 1960s calculators as spin-wave (magnon) recirculating loops in yttrium-iron-garnet films grown by the liquid-phase-epitaxy garnet process of 1980s bubble memory: data rides as spin waves with no charge current and is regenerated by a parametric pump each lap.
why: Energy per access: spin-wave propagation costs aJ per bit versus pJ for charge-based bitlines, >=10x net; garnet LPE needs no EUV and little capital.

title: Intel ETANN Revival: Floating-Gate Analog Weights in Embedded-Flash Fabs
idea: Revive Intel's 1989 80170 ETANN, which stored 10,240 weights as floating-gate charge and multiplied in place: build inference weight banks on U.S. embedded-flash lines (40-28 nm split-gate flash) where weights never leave the array and only accumulated outputs move.
why: Data movement (fact 5): replaces the 3-20 pJ/bit weight fetch with ~10-50 fJ per in-array MAC, >=10x lower energy per effective access, and frees DRAM for activations.

title: Swiss Watch-Chip Subthreshold Design for DRAM Periphery at 0.4 V
idea: Revive Eric Vittoz's 1970s CEH/CSEM watch-chip methodology (subthreshold CMOS for microwatt budgets) for DRAM periphery: decoders, sense-amp control and I/O run at 0.35-0.45 V with body-biased logic and wide, slow, parallel paths replacing fast narrow ones.
why: Periphery (fact 7, ~49% of die) dominates non-array access energy; 1.1 V to 0.4 V cuts CV2 ~7.5x and wide-slow I/O adds more, ~10x overall; transferable to existing fabs as a library change.

title: Bell Labs SEED Smart-Pixels: Free-Space Optical Memory-to-Processor Links
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1980s-90s self-electro-optic-effect device (SEED) smart-pixel arrays: flip-chip a 2D array of quantum-well modulators onto the DRAM die so thousands of bits of an open row beam in parallel through a microlens array onto a photodetector array on the processor, with no SerDes or PHY.
why: Data movement: fJ-class modulators and detectors versus 3-20 pJ/bit electrical I/O, >=10x lower energy per access, and no TSV/HBM base die.

title: IBM System/360 Channel Programs Run Inside the Memory Module
idea: Revive the 1964 S/360 I/O channel, which executed its own channel-command-word programs: CXL memory modules accept CCW-style scatter, gather, filter and top-k programs, walk pointers locally, and return only result bytes to the host.
why: Data movement and overfetch: for pointer chasing, KV lookups and embeddings, 10-100x fewer bits cross the link, >=10x lower energy per useful access, and one module serves more hosts.

title: Goodyear STARAN Associative Search for KV-Cache Recall In DRAM
idea: Revive the 1972 STARAN bit-serial associative array processor: add a 1-bit comparator and match latch to each DRAM sense amplifier so a query key is compared against every stored key in an open row in parallel, and only matching token addresses leave the chip.
why: Energy per useful access: attention retrieval moves only matched KV entries, 10-30x fewer bits off-chip; implemented as a small sense-amp addition on existing DRAM lines.

title: Sun Proximity Communication Revival: Capacitive Face-to-Face Memory Links
idea: Revive Sun Microsystems' 2004 Proximity Communication, where overlapping chip edges exchanged data through capacitive pads microns apart: DRAM dies overlap the accelerator die edge face-to-face in a shingle, passing signals through ~20 um pads with no bumps, TSVs or large drivers.
why: Energy per bit ~0.1-0.3 pJ versus 3-4 pJ (HBM) and 10-20 pJ (DDR5), >=10x lower; removes the TSV tax (fact 6) so standard DRAM wafers suffice.

title: Ramtron EDRAM/Mitsubishi CDRAM: SRAM Row Cache on Every DRAM Bank
idea: Revive the 1990s Enhanced DRAM and Cached DRAM, which put SRAM row caches beside each bank: a 2-4 row SRAM cache per subarray serves repeated hits (hot KV heads, embedding rows) with no activation and lets the DRAM row close at once, reducing activations that also drive row hammer.
why: Hits cost ~0.2-0.5 pJ/bit versus ~5.9 pJ per useful bit for activate-read-restore, ~10x on hit-heavy AI traffic; fabbed on existing DRAM processes.

title: Plated-Wire NDRO Memory Made on Magnet-Wire Lines, Read Without Restore
idea: Revive the plated-wire memory of the UNIVAC 1110 and Viking-era spacecraft (permalloy electroplated on beryllium-copper wire, read non-destructively): continuous wire-plating lines like U.S. magnet-wire plants plate CoFe/NiFe on 25 um wires woven with drive straps, and each read senses only the addressed word's magnetization tilt with a tiny pulse and no restore.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8): word-sized non-destructive reads at ~0.2-0.5 pJ/bit, >=10x below DRAM activate-plus-restore; new supply from the wire industry.

title: Word-Organized Core Revival: 64-Byte Rows Kill DRAM Overfetch
idea: Revive the 1950s linear-select word-organized core memory, where one drive line touched exactly one word: re-architect DRAM mats with segmented local wordlines gated by column select so an activation charges only the 512 cells of one cache line instead of 65,536.
why: Overfetch: activation energy scales with cells opened; 128x fewer cells gives ~10x lower energy per access after periphery, on mature lines with one extra metal layer and no new litho.

title: IBM Thermal Conduction Module Revival: Planar Ceramic DRAM-Compute Modules
idea: Revive IBM's 1980s Thermal Conduction Module, which packed 100+ bare chips on a 33-layer ceramic substrate: place standard non-TSV DRAM dies millimeters from the accelerator on a multilayer glass-ceramic substrate with short, unterminated, wide buses, made by ceramic-package suppliers.
why: Energy per access: unterminated mm-length links at 0.2-0.5 pJ/bit versus 10-20 pJ for DDR5 (>=10x) without HBM's 3x area-per-bit TSV tax; opens a U.S. ceramic-substrate supply route.

title: Matsushita 1995 Charge-Recycling Bus Revived for Memory I/O
idea: Revive Matsushita's mid-1990s charge-recycling bus, which stacked N bus lanes in series voltage domains so charge drained from one lane powers the next: stack 8 DQ lanes between VDDQ and ground so each swings VDDQ/8 and the same charge is reused eight times.
why: I/O energy per bit drops ~8-10x on DDR/LPDDR interfaces (fact 5: 10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5); periphery-only change usable by every DRAM maker.

title: RCA Continuous-Sheet Superconducting Memory Revived in YBCO at 77 K
idea: Revive RCA's 1960s continuous-sheet cryoelectric memory, which stored bits as persistent current vortices in an unpatterned superconducting film at the crossings of drive lines, using high-Tc YBCO films (as made for HTS power cable) at liquid-nitrogen 77 K, so no helium and no cell lithography are needed.
why: Energy per access aJ-fJ, >=10x lower even with LN2 overhead; the storage film is unpatterned so density is set by drive-line pitch on cheap litho; avoids the helium chokepoint.
